newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ's Brash restates comfort with new target.
newsitem.headline: NZ's Brash restates comfort with new target.

text.p: Reserve Bank of New Zealand Governor Don Brash said on Thursday that economists differed on optimal inflation targets but he was comfortable with New Zealand's new zero to three percent range.
"Certainly I had a clear predilection in favour of zero to two (percent) for a long period, but I'm not unhappy with zero to three," Brash said.
He was speaking in an interview with Reuters Financial Television in Washington on whether inflation targets are useful for monetary policy.
The new centre-right coalition government last month widened the central bank's target for underlying inflation to 0-3 percent from 0-2 percent.
Brash said there were two broad schools of thought on whether monetary policy should target low but positive inflation, say one to three percent, or lower inflation still, say 0-2 percent.
The current New Zealand target spanned both of those groups, he said.
Brash said the use of inflation targets had been very successful in the New Zealand context, given the country's poor track record of inflation higher than 10 percent for much of the 1970s and 1980s.
The target had helped to anchor inflation expectations at a low level, he said.
Brash reiterated that the RBNZ expects underlying inflation, which was 2.4 percent in the year to December 1996, to come down in calendar 1997 and into 1998.
"We're projecting the inflation rate moving back towards the middle of our current zero to three target," he said.
Brash stressed that the Reserve Bank's focus remains on price stability under the new agreement he signed last month with Finance Minister Bill Birch, which incorporated the wider inflation target.
Brash said there had been some misunderstanding about whether the bank's mandate had been widened by the new government to target sustainable growth as well as price stability.

"What the agreement actually says is: we should focus on price stability so that monetary policy can make its maximum contribution to growth, employment and so on. The focus remains on price stability," he said.
